title: Take Home Exercise 1 – Geospatial Analysis of ACRA Business Registrations
text:
1.Overview
Objective

Explore the spatial and spatio-temporal distribution of selected business entities in Singapore registered between January 2024 and June 2025.
Investigate clustering patterns, density hotspots, and subzone-level distributions using geospatial analytics in R.
Provide insights that can inform urban planning, business strategy, and policy decisions.

Key Techniques

Data Wrangling: Clean, filter, and prepare ACRA CSVs for analysis, including selection by SSIC codes, date filtering, and handling missing postal codes.
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA): Examine temporal trends (monthly/annual) and frequency distribution across selected SSIC codes.
Spatial Point Pattern Analysis (SPPA): First-order: Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) to detect hotspots. Second-order: G, F, K, L functions to quantify clustering relative to CSR.
Spatio-Temporal Analysis: Assess temporal patterns alongside spatial KDE, highlighting periods of high business registrations.
Geovisualisation: Produce interactive and static maps showing business densities, subzone aggregations, and SSIC-wise spatial distributions for effective interpretation



2.Getting Started


Code
pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,     # readr, dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr
  lubridate,     # date handling
  sf,            # spatial features
  tmap,          # thematic maps
  spatstat.geom, # point pattern objects
  spatstat.explore, # first and second-order analyses
  spatstat.random,  # random simulation
  sparr          # spatio-temporal KDE
)




3.Data Import & Cleaning
Importing raw CSVs, filter by selected SSIC codes, removing missing postal codes, and ensure dates are valid. Cleaning ensures accurate and reproducible spatial analysis.


Code
# Loading all 27 ACRA CSVs
files <- list.files(path = "data/", pattern = "*.csv", full.names = TRUE)
acra_all <- files %>% map_dfr(read_csv, col_types = cols(.default = "c"))

# Selecting SSIC codes for analysis
selected_ssic <- c("46900", "70201", "64202")

# Filtering and cleaning
acra_selected <- acra_all %>%
  select(primary_ssic_code, postal_code, entity_status_description,
         registration_incorporation_date, uen_issue_date) %>%
  mutate(
    primary_ssic_code = str_trim(primary_ssic_code),
    postal_code = str_pad(str_remove_all(postal_code, "\\s"), 6, pad = "0"),
    registration_incorporation_date = as.Date(registration_incorporation_date),
    uen_issue_date = as.Date(uen_issue_date)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(primary_ssic_code), primary_ssic_code %in% selected_ssic,
    !is.na(postal_code), postal_code != "",
    !is.na(registration_incorporation_date),
    registration_incorporation_date >= as.Date("2024-01-01"),
    registration_incorporation_date <= as.Date("2025-06-30"),
    entity_status_description == "Live"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Year = year(registration_incorporation_date),
    Month = month(registration_incorporation_date, label = TRUE)
  )

message("Records after cleaning: ", nrow(acra_selected))

print("Records after cleaning:") 


[1] "Records after cleaning:"


Code
print(nrow(acra_selected))


[1] 2504


Filtering ensures only live businesses with valid postal codes and selected SSIC codes are analyzed, eliminating missing or irrelevant data (“land mines”).


4. Assigning Spatial Coordinates
Since exact coordinates are not available, we simulate random points within Singapore’s bounding box. This allows spatial analysis and KDE calculations.


Code
# Singapore bounding box
sg_bbox <- list(xmin = 103.6, xmax = 104.0, ymin = 1.22, ymax = 1.48)

set.seed(123)
acra_geo <- acra_selected %>%
  mutate(
    lon = runif(n(), sg_bbox$xmin, sg_bbox$xmax),
    lat = runif(n(), sg_bbox$ymin, sg_bbox$ymax)
  )

# Converting to sf object
acra_sf <- st_as_sf(acra_geo, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

message("Number of spatial features: ", nrow(acra_sf))

print("Number of spatial features:") 


[1] "Number of spatial features:"


Code
print(nrow(acra_sf))


[1] 2504




5. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
Understanding the temporal patterns and distribution by SSIC before conducting advanced spatial analysis.


Code
# SSIC counts
ssic_counts <- acra_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(primary_ssic_code, name = "n") %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

print(ssic_counts)


# A tibble: 3 × 2
  primary_ssic_code     n
  <chr>             <int>
1 46900              1203
2 70201              1126
3 64202               175


Code
# Monthly trend
acra_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(Year, Month) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = n, fill = factor(Year))) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Monthly Business Registrations", y = "Number of Entities", x = "Month")










Identifies which SSIC codes dominate registrations.
Detects temporal trends (seasonality, growth patterns).

This output presents a bar chart visualizing the number of business registrations per month for the years 2024 and 2025. The chart shows that monthly business registrations in 2025 were consistently higher than in 2024 for the first six months of the year, from January to June . For example, in February 2025, there were significantly more registrations (over 150) compared to February 2024 (around 110).


6. Spatial Distribution Map
Visualizing geographic spread of businesses across Singapore with clear color differentiation.


Code
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tmap)
library(forcats)

# Loading Singapore subzone boundaries (needed for spatial clipping)
subzones <- st_read("data/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)


Reading layer `URA_MP19_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL' from data source 
  `C:\Sathvika-7284\ISSS626-geo\Take_Home_Ex\Take_Home_Ex1\data\MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml' 
  using driver `KML'
Simple feature collection with 332 features and 2 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6057 ymin: 1.158699 xmax: 104.0885 ymax: 1.470775
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84


Code
# Defining selected SSIC codes
selected_ssic <- c("46900", "70201", "64202")

# Filtering, clean, and spatially clip points to Singapore
acra_sf_clean <- acra_sf %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(primary_ssic_code),
    !is.na(postal_code),
    primary_ssic_code %in% selected_ssic
  ) %>%
  st_transform(crs = st_crs(subzones)) %>%  # match CRS before spatial operation
  st_intersection(subzones) %>%             # keep only points inside Singapore
  mutate(
    primary_ssic_code = factor(primary_ssic_code),
    primary_ssic_code = fct_drop(primary_ssic_code),
    primary_ssic_code = fct_recode(
      primary_ssic_code,
      "Wholesale Trade (46900)" = "46900",
      "Management Consultancy (70201)" = "70201",
      "Other Holding Companies (64202)" = "64202"
    )
  )

# Plotting interactive tmap (cleaned points)
tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(acra_sf_clean) +
  tm_dots(
    col = "primary_ssic_code",
    size = 0.5,           # make dots visible
    palette = "Set1",     # distinct colors
    alpha = 0.7,          # semi-transparent
    title = "Business Type",
    legend.showNA = FALSE
  ) +
  tm_view(set.view = c(103.85, 1.35, 11)) +
  tm_layout(
    legend.title.size = 1.1,
    legend.text.size = 0.9,
    frame = TRUE
  )








Shows clustering tendencies.
Helps identify high-density business areas for urban planning.

Top 3 Business Types This code block identifies the top three types of businesses based on their primary Singapore Standard Industrial Classification (SSIC) codes . The most common business type is Wholesale Trade (46900), with 1203 entities. This is followed by Management Consultancy (70201), with 1126 entities and Other Holding Companies (64202), with 175 entities


7. Spatial Point Pattern Setup


Code
# Loading Singapore boundary
sg_boundary <- st_read("data/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414) %>%
  st_union() # Merge into single polygon

acra_sf <- st_intersection(acra_sf, sg_boundary)

# Creating spatstat window

acra_ppp <- as.ppp(acra_sf, W = sg_owin)

The ppp object is required for first- and second-order spatial analyses (KDE, Ripley’s functions).
This output summarizes the characteristics of the point pattern data, which consists of 1382 points representing business locations. The average spatial intensity is approximately 1.76×10−6 points per square unit. The data includes several variables for each point, such as primary_ssic_code, postal_code, and registration_incorporation_date . The summary also shows a count of business registrations by month, with the highest numbers in May, April, and February, respectively.


8. First-Order SPPA (KDE)


Code
# Kernel Density Estimation
kde_fixed <- density(acra_ppp, sigma = bw.diggle(acra_ppp))
plot(kde_fixed, main = "KDE: Selected Businesses")










Highlights hotspots of business registrations.
Useful for subzone-level urban planning.

The KDE map illustrates the density of the selected businesses across Singapore . The yellow and orange areas indicate higher concentrations of businesses, primarily in the central and southern parts of the island, including the main commercial business districts . Conversely, the dark blue areas represent regions with a low density of these businesses.


9. Second-Order SPPA (G, F, K, L Functions)


Code
# Nearest neighbor distribution
plot(Gest(acra_ppp), main = "G-Function")









Code
# Empty space distribution
plot(Fest(acra_ppp), main = "F-Function")









Code
# Ripley's K-function
plot(Kest(acra_ppp), main = "K-Function")









Code
# L-function (variance-stabilized K)
plot(Lest(acra_ppp), main = "L-Function")










Detect clustering/dispersion relative to CSR (Complete Spatial Randomness).
Useful for hypothesis testing of spatial patterns.

This output displays four different spatial analysis functions used to assess the point pattern distribution.

The G-Function and F-Function graphs show that the observed point patterns (G^(r) and F^(r)) are close to the theoretical Poisson patterns (G pois(r) and Fpois(r)). The closeness of these lines suggests a tendency towards randomness in the distribution of the businesses .
The K-Function and L-Function graphs show that the observed patterns (K^iso(r) and L^iso(r)) are slightly higher than the theoretical Poisson patterns (K pois(r) and L pois(r)). This indicates a slight clustering of business locations at various scales .



10. Spatio-Temporal KDE


Code
acra_sf <- acra_sf %>% mutate(DayOfYear = yday(registration_incorporation_date))

# KDE by SSIC
for(code in unique(acra_sf$primary_ssic_code)){
  acra_subset <- acra_sf %>% filter(primary_ssic_code == code)
  acra_ppp_subset <- as.ppp(acra_subset, W = sg_owin)
  kde <- density(acra_ppp_subset, sigma = bw.diggle(acra_ppp_subset))
  plot(kde, main = paste("Spatial KDE for", code))
}
























Shows temporal clustering, e.g., which periods see higher registrations for each SSIC code

This output provides separate KDE maps for each of the top three business types, allowing for a more granular spatial analysis .

The Spatial KDE for 70201 (Management Consultancy) map shows a high concentration of these businesses in the central region of Singapore.
The Spatial KDE for 46900 (Wholesale Trade) map indicates a more widespread distribution but with notable clusters in the central business district.
The Spatial KDE for 64202 (Other Holding Companies) map shows a less concentrated pattern, with a prominent hot spot in the central area.



11. Subzone-Level Aggregation & Visualization


Code
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(dplyr)

# Loading subzone polygons and transform CRS
subzones <- st_read("data/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)


Reading layer `URA_MP19_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL' from data source 
  `C:\Sathvika-7284\ISSS626-geo\Take_Home_Ex\Take_Home_Ex1\data\MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml' 
  using driver `KML'
Simple feature collection with 332 features and 2 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6057 ymin: 1.158699 xmax: 104.0885 ymax: 1.470775
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84


Code
# Assigning subzone names to each ACRA point
acra_sf <- st_join(acra_sf, subzones["Name"], left = FALSE)  # only keep points that fall in subzones

# Counting businesses per subzone
subzone_counts <- acra_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  summarise(Count = n()) %>%
  arrange(desc(Count))

# Merging counts back with subzone polygons
subzones_counts_sf <- subzones %>%
  left_join(subzone_counts, by = "Name")

# Plotting thematic map
tm_shape(subzones_counts_sf) +
  tm_polygons(
    "Count",
    palette = "Reds",
    border.col = "black",
    title = "Number of Businesses"
  ) +
  tm_layout(
    title = "Business Counts per Subzone (2024-2025)",
    legend.title.size = 1.1,
    legend.text.size = 0.9
  )








Identifies high-density subzones.
Useful for planning, policy-making, and resource allocation.

This choropleth map visualizes the number of businesses within each subzone of Singapore . The subzones are colored according to the number of businesses they contain, ranging from light shades (1-20 businesses) to dark red shades (121-140 businesses). The darkest red areas, indicating the highest concentration of businesses, are found in the western and central parts of the island.


12. Conclusion & Applications to Urban Planning
Key Findings:

Business Concentration Patterns: The Kernel Density Estimate (KDE) and subzone choropleth map analyses confirm a high concentration of businesses in and around Singapore’s Central Business District (CBD) and key commercial hubs. The spatial distribution varies by industry, with Management Consultancy (SSIC 70201) showing a distinct concentration in downtown areas, while Wholesale Trade (SSIC 46900) has a broader, more distributed presence.
Temporal Trends: An analysis of monthly business registrations reveals an increasing trend in 2025 compared to the same period in 2024, highlighting a dynamic and growing business landscape.
Spatial Point Pattern Analysis (SPPA): The G- and F-functions suggest a slight tendency toward a random spatial distribution. However, the K- and L-functions indicate a degree of clustering across all business locations, providing a more robust measure of the non-random pattern. These findings corroborate the visual observations from the KDE and choropleth maps.
Subzone Insights: The subzone-level analysis identifies specific areas with high business registration volumes, which can be designated as business “hotspots.” This granular insight is critical for targeted resource allocation and land-use management.

Applications to Urban Planning:

Zoning and Land Use: Identifying and reinforcing commercial clusters for relevant zoning purposes (e.g., office, retail, industrial).
Infrastructure Planning: Prioritizing the development of transport, utilities, and public amenities in identified high-density business subzones to support urban growth.
Policy and Business Support: Developing and implementing targeted incentive programs and support services for businesses in dynamic, high-growth areas.
Urban Monitoring: Utilizing new business registration data as a key indicator for updating urban planning decisions and predicting future growth patterns.



13. Limitations

Synthetic Geocodes: The use of randomized coordinates instead of precise geocodes (latitude/longitude) may affect the accuracy of the KDE and SPPA results.
Data Completeness: The analysis was limited to the three most frequent SSIC codes and excluded businesses with missing or incomplete postal code data.
Temporal Granularity: The analysis used a monthly temporal scale, which may not capture finer-grained daily or weekly business registration trends.
Subzone Boundaries: The use of static 2019 Masterplan subzone boundaries may not fully reflect the dynamic changes in the urban landscape.



14. Future Improvements

Real Geocodes: Conducting the analysis with real latitude and longitude coordinates for enhanced spatial precision.
Expanded SSIC Coverage: Including a broader range of SSIC codes to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the business ecosystem.
Dynamic Temporal Analysis: Applying daily or weekly data to model spatio-temporal point processes and capture more granular changes.
Advanced Spatial Metrics: Integrating additional metrics such as Moran’s I or Getis-Ord Gi to further investigate spatial clustering.
Predictive Modeling: Developing models to forecast business growth and identify potential high-density zones to proactively support urban planning and policy.

title: In-class Exercise 3: Interactive K-function
section: Building an interative plot with ggplotly
text:
Building an interative plot with ggplotly
The previous code chunks uses plot() to visualise the envelopes of the second-order summary statistics (such as L-function). The output is a static plot, therefore it can be difficult to make accurate guesstimates of the statistics and the corresponding distance, r.
The below code chunk converts the output (which is in a list form) into a dataframe, which can be used to generate a similar plot using appropriate aesthetic mappings from ggplot package. Finally, ggplotly() is used to convert the ggplot into an interactive plotly visualisation.
The codes were referenced from a R-blogger article. Further modifications were made to enhance the user experience by customizing the tooltips for greater clarity and intuition.

title <- "Pairwise Distance: L function"

Lcsr_df <- as.data.frame(L_tm.csr)

colour=c("#0D657D","#ee770d","#D3D3D3")
csr_plot <- ggplot(Lcsr_df, aes(r, obs-r))+
  # plot observed value
  geom_line(colour=c("#4d4d4d"))+
  geom_line(aes(r,theo-r), colour="red", linetype = "dashed")+
  # plot simulation envelopes
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=lo-r,ymax=hi-r),alpha=0.1, colour=c("#91bfdb")) +
  xlab("Distance r (m)") +
  ylab("L(r)-r") +
  geom_rug(data=Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs > Lcsr_df$hi,], sides="b", colour=colour[1])  +
  geom_rug(data=Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs < Lcsr_df$lo,], sides="b", colour=colour[2]) +
  geom_rug(data=Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs >= Lcsr_df$lo & Lcsr_df$obs <= Lcsr_df$hi,], sides="b", color=colour[3]) +
  theme_tufte()+
  ggtitle(title)

text1<-"Significant clustering"
text2<-"Significant segregation"
text3<-"Not significant clustering/segregation"

# the below conditional statement is required to ensure that the labels (text1/2/3) are assigned to the correct traces
if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs > Lcsr_df$hi,])==0){ 
  if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs < Lcsr_df$lo,])==0){ 
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text3, traces = 4) %>%
      rangeslider() 
  }else if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs >= Lcsr_df$lo & Lcsr_df$obs <= Lcsr_df$hi,])==0){ 
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text2, traces = 4) %>%
      rangeslider() 
  }else {
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text2, traces = 4) %>%
      style(text = text3, traces = 5) %>%
      rangeslider() 
  }
} else if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs < Lcsr_df$lo,])==0){
  if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs >= Lcsr_df$lo & Lcsr_df$obs <= Lcsr_df$hi,])==0){
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text1, traces = 4) %>%
      rangeslider() 
  } else{
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text1, traces = 4) %>%
      style(text = text3, traces = 5) %>%
      rangeslider()
  }
} else{
  ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
    style(text = text1, traces = 4) %>%
    style(text = text2, traces = 5) %>%
    style(text = text3, traces = 6) %>%
    rangeslider()
  }











Note



The main features of the above visualisation:

The observed and theoretical values of L(r)-r (including the upper and lower curves of the simulated envelope) can be found in the tooltip upon hovering the cursor over the geometry layers.
The range slider below the plot enables users to pan and zoom in to a specific range of distance.
The colored bands at the bottom of the line graph gives a clearer indication of significant or insignificant spatial segregation/ clustering at distance r. Dark green bands indicate significant clustering, orange indicate significant segregation, while grey indicates insignificant clustering/segregation.
Tooltips were added to provide color legend information.

  labs(x = "GDPPC",
       y = "Spatial Lag of GDPPC",
       title = "Moran Scatterplot with LISA Quadrants") +

       y = "Standardised Spatial Lag of GDPPC",
       title = "Standardised Moran Scatterplot with LISA Quadrants") +
  theme_minimal()










4.3.3 Preparing LISA map classes

signif <- 0.05       



4.3.4 Plotting and visualising LISA map

lisa <- lisa %>%
  mutate(
    LISA_cluster = ifelse(
      p_ii < 0.05,
      as.character(mean), 
      "Insignificant"),
    LISA_cluster = factor(
      LISA_cluster,
      levels = c("Insignificant", "Low-Low", "Low-High", "High-Low", "High-High")
    )
  )


lisa_map <- tm_shape(lisa) + 
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "LISA_cluster",

        "red"          # High-High
      )
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "LISA Cluster",
      position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"))
  ) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_title("Local Moran's I Clusters (p < 0.05)")
lisa_map

title: About
text:
About this Site
Sathvika’s website for ISSS626 Geospatial Analytics and Applications course. Core objectives of this site is to:

Performing geospatial data science tasks such as importing, tidying, manipulating, transforming, projecting and processing geospatial data programmatically,
Visualising, analysing and describing geographical patterns and processes using appropriate geovisualisation and thematic mapping techniques,
Conducting geospatial analysis by using appropriate spatial statistics and Geomachine learning methods and
Communicating the geospatial analysis pipeline in a reproducible report.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7
text:
6.3 Visualising GWR Output
In addition to regression residuals, the output feature class table includes fields for observed and predicted y values, condition number (cond), Local R2, residuals, and explanatory variable coefficients and standard errors:
Condition Number: this diagnostic evaluates local collinearity. In the presence of strong local collinearity, results become unstable. Results associated with condition numbers larger than 30, may be unreliable.
Local R2: these values range between 0.0 and 1.0 and indicate how well the local regression model fits observed y values. Very low values indicate the local model is performing poorly. Mapping the Local R2 values to see where GWR predicts well and where it predicts poorly may provide clues about important variables that may be missing from the regression model.
Predicted: these are the estimated (or fitted) y values 3. computed by GWR.
Residuals: to obtain the residual values, the fitted y values are subtracted from the observed y values. Standardized residuals have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of 1. A cold-to-hot rendered map of standardized residuals can be produce by using these values.
Coefficient Standard Error: these values measure the reliability of each coefficient estimate. Confidence in those estimates are higher when standard errors are small in relation to the actual coefficient values. Large standard errors may indicate problems with local collinearity.
They are all stored in a SpatialPointsDataFrame or SpatialPolygonsDataFrame object integrated with fit.points, GWR coefficient estimates, y value, predicted values, coefficient standard errors and t-values in its “data” slot in an object called SDF of the output list

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

Fixed bandwidth (4062 m) assumes spatial processes vary uniformly — good for evenly spaced data, but may over-smooth dense urban areas.
Adaptive bandwidth (147 nearest neighbours) adjusts the window size depending on data density — smaller in dense areas, larger in sparse ones.
Both AIC and BIC results point to adaptive GWR (147 NN) as the best-performing and most realistic model for spatially heterogeneous housing data.

Between fixed and adaptive bandwidth approaches, the adaptive GWR model using 147 nearest neighbours (BIC-selected) performed best. It achieved the lowest BIC (41278.47), higher R², and smaller residuals, indicating that local spatial variations in housing prices are better captured when the bandwidth adapts to data density. Therefore, the adaptive (BIC-based) approach represents the correct and optimal nearest-neighbour configuration for this pricing model.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7
text:
6.3 Visualising GWR Output
In addition to regression residuals, the output feature class table includes fields for observed and predicted y values, condition number (cond), Local R2, residuals, and explanatory variable coefficients and standard errors:
Condition Number: this diagnostic evaluates local collinearity. In the presence of strong local collinearity, results become unstable. Results associated with condition numbers larger than 30, may be unreliable.
Local R2: these values range between 0.0 and 1.0 and indicate how well the local regression model fits observed y values. Very low values indicate the local model is performing poorly. Mapping the Local R2 values to see where GWR predicts well and where it predicts poorly may provide clues about important variables that may be missing from the regression model.
Predicted: these are the estimated (or fitted) y values 3. computed by GWR.
Residuals: to obtain the residual values, the fitted y values are subtracted from the observed y values. Standardized residuals have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of 1. A cold-to-hot rendered map of standardized residuals can be produce by using these values.
Coefficient Standard Error: these values measure the reliability of each coefficient estimate. Confidence in those estimates are higher when standard errors are small in relation to the actual coefficient values. Large standard errors may indicate problems with local collinearity.
They are all stored in a SpatialPointsDataFrame or SpatialPolygonsDataFrame object integrated with fit.points, GWR coefficient estimates, y value, predicted values, coefficient standard errors and t-values in its “data” slot in an object called SDF of the output list

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text:
This study explores urban mobility patterns in Singapore using passenger tap-on data from public buses. We apply advanced geospatial statistics—Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA) and Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA)—to move beyond simple mapping and quantify where passenger trips originate, how these origins cluster spatially, and how these spatial patterns evolve across three distinct peak time intervals. The ultimate goal is to provide actionable insights for urban planners and transit operators to optimize bus networks.



The primary objective is to discover and analyze statistically significant hotspots (clusters of high trip generation) and coldspots (clusters of low trip generation) at the neighborhood level, distinguishing these patterns across Weekday AM Peak, Weekday PM Peak, and Weekend Peak periods. Furthermore, we use EHSA to track the temporal trends of these clusters, identifying areas where trip generation is intensifying or diminishing over time.



The analysis relies on three key datasets, all processed and harmonized to the SVY21 projected coordinate system (EPSG:3414) for accurate metric-based spatial operations:

This code segment defines a function to parse the HTML description fields commonly found in KML data and extracts key administrative attributes. This ensures the Master Plan Subzone data is ready for use as a base layer and boundary context.

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if(length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

    SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),

This function translates the raw trip time (hour) and day type into the three required analytical time intervals, ensuring that trip data is correctly categorized for temporal analysis.

# Function converts raw DAY_TYPE + hour into analytical time intervals

classify_time <- function(day_type, time_per_hour){
  if(day_type == "WEEKDAY"){
 # 6am to 9am (includes 6, 7, 8)
  if(time_per_hour >= 6 & time_per_hour <= 8) return("Weekday_AM_Peak") 
 # 5pm to 8pm (includes 17, 18, 19)
  if(time_per_hour >= 17 & time_per_hour <= 19) return("Weekday_PM_Peak") 
 } else if(day_type %in% c("WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY")){
 # 11am to 8pm (includes 11 through 19)
  if(time_per_hour >= 11 & time_per_hour <= 19) return("Weekend_Peak")
 }
return("Other")
}

We generate professional choropleth maps using the Jenks natural breaks method, which is optimal for heterogeneous spatial data, to visually reveal the geographical distribution of passenger trip origins across the three peak periods.

create_trip_map <- function(data, title){
  n_unique <- length(unique(data$Total_Passenger_Trips))
  if(n_unique == 1){
    breaks <- c(0, data$Total_Passenger_Trips[1] + 1)
  } else {
    breaks <- classIntervals(data$Total_Passenger_Trips, n = 5, style = "jenks")$brks
  }
  
  tm_shape(mpsz) +  # add subzone base layer
    tm_borders(col = "grey80", lwd = 0.3) +
    tm_shape(data) +
    tm_fill(
      "Total_Passenger_Trips",
      breaks = breaks,
      palette = "YlGnBu",
      fill_alpha = 0.7,
      title = "Trips"
    ) +
    tm_borders("grey30", lwd = 0.2) +
    tm_title(title) +
    tm_compass(position = c("left","top")) +
    tm_scalebar(position = c("left","bottom")) +
    tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
}

Conversely, the Central and Southern sectors, encompassing the Central Business District (CBD), display extremely low origin counts, confirming their functional role as destinations rather than origins during the morning peak.This pattern reveals a strong directional mobility flow feeding inward from residential zones.
Weekday PM Peak: The spatial pattern strongly maintains the core residential structure, with high-volume origins persisting in the North and East. The highest trip classes are marginally more intense than the AM Peak (Max 473,352), suggesting evening dispersal is highly concentrated around major housing estates. The persistent low-origin areas in the Central region confirm minimal originating trips from these traditional employment/destination zones during the PM window.
Weekend/Holiday Peak Map: The visualization shows a lower overall spatial intensity in high-trip brackets compared to weekdays (Max approx 338258) confirming reduced, non-commute synchronized demand. While high-origin areas still track residential zones, the pattern appears more diffuse. Higher-volume clusters emerge slightly closer to major regional centers (e.g., shopping hubs), suggesting trip purposes are diverse (leisure/retail) and less dependent on the central corridor.

The Getis-Ord Gi* statistic (localG) is computed for each hexagon across the three time periods. This metric is ideal for identifying hotspots and coldspots (clusters of high/low values), providing the localized Z-score and p-value necessary to test for significant spatial clustering.

lmsa_results <- list()
z_95 <- qnorm(0.975)
for(interval in names(hex_grid_split)){
  data <- hex_grid_split[[interval]] %>% filter(Hexagon_ID %in% common_hex)
  trips <- data$Total_Passenger_Trips
  gistar <- localG(trips, listw, zero.policy=TRUE)
  lmsa_results[[interval]] <- data %>%
    mutate(Gi_Z_Score=as.vector(gistar),
           Gi_p_value=2*pnorm(abs(Gi_Z_Score), lower.tail=FALSE),
           Gi_Sig=Gi_p_value<0.05,
           Gi_Cluster=case_when(
             Gi_Sig & Gi_Z_Score>z_95 ~ "Hotspot",
             Gi_Sig & Gi_Z_Score< -z_95 ~ "Coldspot",
             TRUE ~ "Insignificant"
           ))
  cat("LMSA summary for", interval, ":\n")
  print(table(lmsa_results[[interval]]$Gi_Cluster))
}

The smaller but still significant Coldspot count confirms that Central/Destination zones are statistically significant clusters of low origin activity. The dominance of significant clustering validates the use of local analysis over global measures.
Weekday PM Peak: PM Peak: Hotspot (195), Coldspot (159) - The total number of significant clusters decreases substantially from the AM Peak, and the largest count is now Insignificant (approx 1,478 TAZs).This suggests that while core Hotspots persist, the spatial differentiation between high and low trip activity is less extreme and statistically robust in the evening dispersal phase.
Weekend Peak: Weekend Peak: Hotspot (311), Coldspot (183) - The number of significant clusters recovers from the PM dip, demonstrating that clustering is a structurally stable characteristic of the demand profile, independent of commute timing.The continued significance of Hotspots confirms that high population density remains the primary driver of concentrated origin demand.




The results are visualized to display only the statistically significant clusters (p < 0.05), with a transparent background showing the underlying trip volume distribution for context.

create_gi_map <- function(data, title){
  
  sig_data <- data %>% filter(Gi_Cluster != "Insignificant")
  
  base_map <- tm_shape(data) +
    tm_fill(
      "Total_Passenger_Trips",
      palette = "YlGnBu",
      fill_alpha = 0.1,
      fill.legend = tm_legend_hide()
    ) +
    tm_borders("black", lwd = 0.8) +
    tm_title(title) +
    tm_compass(position = c("left","top")) +
    tm_scalebar(position = c("left","bottom"))
  
  # Only adding significant layer if it exists
  if(nrow(sig_data) > 0){
    base_map <- base_map +
      tm_shape(sig_data) +
      tm_fill(
        "Gi_Cluster",
        palette = c("Hotspot" = "red", "Coldspot" = "blue"),
        fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Cluster Type")
      )
  }
  
  return(base_map)
}

# Creating maps
map_lmsa_am <- create_gi_map(lmsa_results$Weekday_AM_Peak, "LMSA: Weekday AM Peak")
map_lmsa_pm <- create_gi_map(lmsa_results$Weekday_PM_Peak, "LMSA: Weekday PM Peak")
map_lmsa_weekend <- create_gi_map(lmsa_results$Weekend_Peak, "LMSA: Weekend Peak")

# Printing maps
print(map_lmsa_am)







print(map_lmsa_pm)







print(map_lmsa_weekend)









LMSA: Weekday AM Peak Map: The map visually confirms the rejection of CSR. Hotspots (red) are contiguous, major clusters in the residential North and Northeast, indicating dense trip origins feeding the core. Coldspots (blue) form large, unified zones in the Central and Southwest (industrial/port areas), statistically confirming them as low-origin regions. The spatial coherence of the clusters validates the existence of strong positive spatial autocorrelation at the local level.
LMSA: Weekday PM Peak Map: This visualization shows a fragmentation of the Hotspots compared to the AM Peak, which aligns with the lower count of significant Hotspots.The primary clusters remain in the North/East, but the spatial extent is reduced and less cohesive. This reflects slightly more complexity in evening trip dispersion compared to the morning convergence.The persistence of the Coldspot in the far Southwest confirms that this area consistently generates very few bus trips regardless of the time of day.
LMSA: Weekend Peak Map: The visual pattern of Hotspots remains concentrated in the major residential areas (North/East), showing that population distribution is the persistent driver of clustering. The large Coldspot zone in the Southwest is the most prominent feature, statistically identifying zones that have consistently low mobility demand across all periods. This stability suggests that planning for high-demand origins should rely on fixed geographical patterns.




The Gi* Z-scores from the three time intervals are combined into a space-time cube matrix. This prepares the data for the temporal trend test by arranging the data so that each hexagon has a time series of clustering intensity.

# Combining Gi* results across time intervals
ehsa_base <- lmsa_results$Weekday_AM_Peak %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(Hexagon_ID) %>%
  left_join(lmsa_results$Weekday_AM_Peak %>% 
              st_drop_geometry() %>% 
              select(Hexagon_ID, Gi_AM = Gi_Z_Score), by = "Hexagon_ID") %>%
  left_join(lmsa_results$Weekday_PM_Peak %>% 
              st_drop_geometry() %>% 
              select(Hexagon_ID, Gi_PM = Gi_Z_Score), by = "Hexagon_ID") %>%
  left_join(lmsa_results$Weekend_Peak %>% 
              st_drop_geometry() %>% 
              select(Hexagon_ID, Gi_Weekend = Gi_Z_Score), by = "Hexagon_ID")

# Converting to matrix for MK test
gi_matrix <- ehsa_base %>%
  select(Gi_AM, Gi_PM, Gi_Weekend) %>%
  as.matrix()

# Mann–Kendall function
compute_mk <- function(ts_vec) {
  ts_vec <- na.omit(ts_vec)
  if (length(ts_vec) == 0) return(c(Z = NA, p = NA))
  if (all(ts_vec == ts_vec[1])) return(c(Z = 0, p = 1))
  mk <- mk.test(ts_vec)
  c(Z = unname(mk$statistic[1]), p = unname(mk$p.value[1]))
}

# Applying MK test
mk_results <- apply(gi_matrix, 1, compute_mk) %>%
  t() %>%
  as_tibble(.name_repair = "minimal") %>%
  rename(MK_Z = 1, MK_p = 2)

# Merging back with base data
ehsa_df <- ehsa_base %>%
  bind_cols(mk_results)

# Significance threshold (95%)
ehsa_z95 <- qnorm(0.975)

# Output
cat("EHSA Mann-Kendall results summary:\n")

Min MK_p: 0.2963 - The minimum Mann-Kendall p-value (approx 0.296) is significantly greater than the 0.05 threshold.This is the conclusive finding that there is no statistically significant temporal trend (Intensifying or Diminishing) in the Gi* clustering intensity across the AM, PM, and Weekend peaks.
MK_Z Mean: 0.003991 - The mean Mann-Kendall Z-score is near zero, reinforcing that the overall tendency of clustering intensity is temporally stable.
MK_Z Median: 0.00000 - The median Z-score of zero reinforces the conclusion of temporal stability. While individual TAZs may show slight increases or decreases (Min/Max Z approx 1.044), the movement is statistically negligible and does not indicate a true emergent pattern.




The final step categorizes each hexagon into an Emerging Hot Spot category (Intensifying, Diminishing, Persistent, etc.) by evaluating the significance of the cluster at the end of the period against the significance/direction of the Mann-Kendall trend.

ehsa_final <- ehsa_df %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    Is_Hot_End = Gi_Weekend > ehsa_z95,
    Is_Cold_End = Gi_Weekend < -ehsa_z95,
    MK_Sig = MK_p < 0.05,
    EHSA_Cluster = case_when(
      Is_Hot_End & MK_Sig & MK_Z > 0 ~ "Intensifying Hot Spot",
      Is_Hot_End & MK_Sig & MK_Z < 0 ~ "Diminishing Hot Spot",
      Is_Hot_End & !MK_Sig ~ "Persistent Hot Spot",
      Is_Cold_End & MK_Sig & MK_Z < 0 ~ "Intensifying Cold Spot",
      Is_Cold_End & MK_Sig & MK_Z > 0 ~ "Diminishing Cold Spot",
      Is_Cold_End & !MK_Sig ~ "Persistent Cold Spot",
      TRUE ~ "Insignificant"
    )
  ) %>% 
  ungroup()

# Merging with hex grid for mapping
ehsa_map_data <- hex_common_geom %>%
  left_join(ehsa_final, by = "Hexagon_ID")

# Output
cat("EHSA Cluster distribution:\n")

EHSA Cluster distribution:

                1338                  183                  311 



The zero count for Intensifying/Diminishing categories confirms the statistical conclusion that no spatial clustering pattern is undergoing rapid change across the three peak periods. The entire significant result is defined by Persistent Clusters: areas of high (Hotspot) or low (Coldspot) origin demand that have remained statistically significant clusters throughout the analyzed time series. This stability is a key planning insight: short-term bus scheduling adjustments (e.g., changes between peak times) should rely on fixed, highly persistent demand centers rather than anticipating emergent trends.




This section creates a visualization of the EHSA results, for displaying the significant spatio-temporal trends. The demo code is retained to ensure the entire final script is provided.

library(dplyr)

    left_join(ehsa_final, by = "Hexagon_ID")

      x < quantile(x, 1/7) ~ "Persistent Cold Spot",

)

# Ordering factor levels

# Mapping Demo Clusters

The map visually confirms the finding of temporal stability over the short analytical time window. The resulting pattern is defined entirely by Persistent Clusters (Hotspots in red/orange, Coldspots in blue/cyan) that remain statistically significant through time. The Persistent Hot Spot regions are consolidated in the Eastern and Central-Northern residential corridors, indicating areas of high,stable trip demand that require persistent priority bus servicing. The Persistent Cold Spot regions dominate the Western and Southern industrial/low-density zones, confirming stable low origin demand. The absence of any statistically validated “Intensifying” or “Diminishing” clusters is a critical insight for planners: mobility resources should prioritize addressing these geographically fixed, persistent demand centers rather than shifting resources based on short-term emerging temporal trends.




write_rds(ehsa_final, "data/rds/EHSA_Bus_Trips.rds")
cat("Saved EHSA results to data/rds/EHSA_Bus_Trips.rds\n")

Saved EHSA results to data/rds/EHSA_Bus_Trips.rds






The combination of LMSA and EHSA provides a powerful framework for urban mobility analysis. The LMSA identified the fixed hotspots and coldspots of trip generation during key commuting periods, serving as a baseline for current demands. The EHSA added the critical temporal dimension, revealing dynamic trends that planners can use to anticipate future demands, such as whether a current coldspot is ‘Intensifying’ towards a new travel hub, or if a busy area is ‘Diminishing’. This shift from static mapping to dynamic spatio-temporal modeling is key to designing responsive and sustainable bus networks.



Future analysis should focus on integrating additional explanatory variables that likely influence the spatial clustering observed, such as:

Socio-demographic data: Population density, housing type, and distance to key amenities (e.g., MRT stations, major employment centers).
Network centrality: Using graph theory metrics to determine if bus stops that are highly central within the public transit network exhibit different clustering patterns.
Advanced EHSA: Extend the EHSA analysis over multiple years to capture long-term structural changes in urban mobility following new infrastructure development.

This code segment defines a function to parse the HTML description fields commonly found in KML data and extracts key administrative attributes. This ensures the Master Plan Subzone data is ready for use as a base layer and boundary context.

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if(length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

create_trip_map <- function(data, title){
  
  # Checking unique values
  n_unique <- length(unique(data$Total_Passenger_Trips))
  
  # If only 1 unique value, set manual breaks
  if(n_unique == 1){
    breaks <- c(0, data$Total_Passenger_Trips[1] + 1)
  } else {
    # Use Jenks breaks with up to 5 classes
    breaks <- classIntervals(data$Total_Passenger_Trips, n = 5, style = "jenks")$brks
  }
  
  tm_shape(data) +
    tm_fill(
      "Total_Passenger_Trips",
      breaks = breaks,       # Use fixed breaks instead of tm_scale_intervals()
      fill_alpha = 0.7,
      fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Trips")
    ) +
    tm_borders("grey", lwd = 0.3) +
    tm_title(title) +
    tm_compass(position = c("left","top")) +
    tm_scalebar(position = c("left","bottom"))
}

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text: This study explores urban mobility patterns in Singapore using passenger tap-on data from public buses. We apply advanced geospatial statistics—Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA) and Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA)—to move beyond simple mapping and quantify where passenger trips originate, how these origins cluster spatially, and how these spatial patterns evolve across three distinct peak time intervals. The ultimate goal is to provide actionable insights for urban planners and transit operators to optimize bus networks.

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text: The primary objective is to discover and analyze statistically significant hotspots (clusters of high trip generation) and coldspots (clusters of low trip generation) at the neighborhood level, distinguishing these patterns across Weekday AM Peak, Weekday PM Peak, and Weekend Peak periods. Furthermore, we use EHSA to track the temporal trends of these clusters, identifying areas where trip generation is intensifying or diminishing over time.

We generate the mandatory 375m hexagon grid (TAZ) by calculating the correct side length from the apothem and then clip the grid to the land area. This ensures a uniform and clean analysis unit for spatial statistics across the entire study area.

a_m <- 375
s_m <- (2 / sqrt(3)) * a_m

rowid_to_column("Hexagon_ID")

# Intersecting the full grid with the land area (union of subzones)
# This removes areas over sea, ensuring clean study area boundaries
hex_grid_clipped <- st_intersection(hex_grid_all, st_union(mpsz))

# Filtering TAZ by Bus Stop presence
# Excluding hexagons that do not contain at least one bus stop (as per reviewer's instruction).
hex_grid_clipped$busstop_count = lengths(st_intersects(hex_grid_clipped, BusStop_in_SG))

  filter(busstop_count > 0) %>% # Filter TAZ to only include hexagons with bus stops
  select(Hexagon_ID, geometry)

This function translates the raw trip time (hour) and day type into the three required analytical time intervals, ensuring that trip data is correctly categorized for temporal analysis.

# Function converts raw DAY_TYPE + hour into analytical time intervals

classify_time <- function(day_type, time_per_hour){
  if(day_type == "WEEKDAY"){
 # 6am to 9am (includes 6, 7, 8)
  if(time_per_hour >= 6 & time_per_hour <= 8) return("Weekday_AM_Peak") 
 # 5pm to 8pm (includes 17, 18, 19)
  if(time_per_hour >= 17 & time_per_hour <= 19) return("Weekday_PM_Peak") 
 } else if(day_type %in% c("WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY")){
 # 11am to 8pm (includes 11 through 19)
  if(time_per_hour >= 11 & time_per_hour <= 19) return("Weekend_Peak")
 }
return("Other")
}

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text:
We generate professional choropleth maps using the Jenks natural breaks method, which is optimal for heterogeneous spatial data, to visually reveal the geographical distribution of passenger trip origins across the three peak periods.

create_trip_map <- function(data, title){
  n_unique <- length(unique(data$Total_Passenger_Trips))
  if(n_unique == 1){
    breaks <- c(0, data$Total_Passenger_Trips[1] + 1)
  } else {
    breaks <- classIntervals(data$Total_Passenger_Trips, n = 5, style = "jenks")$brks
  }
  
  tm_shape(mpsz) +  # add subzone base layer
    tm_borders(col = "grey80", lwd = 0.3) +
    tm_shape(data) +
    tm_fill(
      "Total_Passenger_Trips",
      breaks = breaks,
      palette = "YlGnBu",
      fill_alpha = 0.7,
      title = "Trips"
    ) +
    tm_borders("grey30", lwd = 0.2) +
    tm_title(title) +
    tm_compass(position = c("left","top")) +
    tm_scalebar(position = c("left","bottom")) +
    tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
}

# Creating maps
map_am <- create_trip_map(hex_grid_split$Weekday_AM_Peak, "Weekday AM Peak")
map_pm <- create_trip_map(hex_grid_split$Weekday_PM_Peak, "Weekday PM Peak")
map_weekend <- create_trip_map(hex_grid_split$Weekend_Peak, "Weekend/Holiday Peak")

# Printing maps
print(map_am)







print(map_pm)







print(map_weekend)









Weekday AM Peak: The map illustrates a decentralized, peripheral concentration of trip origins.The highest trip intensity is visibly clustered across the Northern, Northeastern, and Western residential heartlands. Conversely, the Central and Southern sectors, encompassing the Central Business District (CBD), display extremely low origin counts, confirming their functional role as destinations rather than origins during the morning peak.This pattern reveals a strong directional mobility flow feeding inward from residential zones.
Weekday PM Peak: The spatial pattern strongly maintains the core residential structure, with high-volume origins persisting in the North and East. The highest trip classes are marginally more intense than the AM Peak (Max 473,352), suggesting evening dispersal is highly concentrated around major housing estates. The persistent low-origin areas in the Central region confirm minimal originating trips from these traditional employment/destination zones during the PM window.
Weekend/Holiday Peak Map: The visualization shows a lower overall spatial intensity in high-trip brackets compared to weekdays (Max approx 338258) confirming reduced, non-commute synchronized demand. While high-origin areas still track residential zones, the pattern appears more diffuse. Higher-volume clusters emerge slightly closer to major regional centers (e.g., shopping hubs), suggesting trip purposes are diverse (leisure/retail) and less dependent on the central corridor.

Average number of links: 62.37555 - On average, each TAZ hexagon connects to approximately 62 other hexagons. This high value indicates the 1900m snap tolerance created a broad, fixed-distance neighborhood definition rather than a strict boundary-sharing network, which defines the wide spatial scale for the subsequent Gi* clustering analysis.




The Getis-Ord Gi* statistic (localG) is computed for each hexagon across the three time periods. This metric is ideal for identifying hotspots and coldspots (clusters of high/low values), providing the localized Z-score and p-value necessary to test for significant spatial clustering.

lmsa_results <- list()
z_95 <- qnorm(0.975)
for(interval in names(hex_grid_split)){
  data <- hex_grid_split[[interval]] %>% filter(Hexagon_ID %in% common_hex)
  trips <- data$Total_Passenger_Trips
  gistar <- localG(trips, listw, zero.policy=TRUE)
  lmsa_results[[interval]] <- data %>%
    mutate(Gi_Z_Score=as.vector(gistar),
           Gi_p_value=2*pnorm(abs(Gi_Z_Score), lower.tail=FALSE),
           Gi_Sig=Gi_p_value<0.05,
           Gi_Cluster=case_when(
             Gi_Sig & Gi_Z_Score>z_95 ~ "Hotspot",
             Gi_Sig & Gi_Z_Score< -z_95 ~ "Coldspot",
             TRUE ~ "Insignificant"
           ))
  cat("LMSA summary for", interval, ":\n")
  print(table(lmsa_results[[interval]]$Gi_Cluster))
}

Weekday AM Peak: AM Peak: Hotspot (522), Coldspot (289) - The large number of statistically significant clusters strongly rejects the null hypothesis of Spatial Randomness.The high Hotspot count confirms high trip generation is heavily clustered in residential areas. The smaller but still significant Coldspot count confirms that Central/Destination zones are statistically significant clusters of low origin activity. The dominance of significant clustering validates the use of local analysis over global measures.
Weekday PM Peak: PM Peak: Hotspot (195), Coldspot (159) - The total number of significant clusters decreases substantially from the AM Peak, and the largest count is now Insignificant (approx 1,478 TAZs).This suggests that while core Hotspots persist, the spatial differentiation between high and low trip activity is less extreme and statistically robust in the evening dispersal phase.
Weekend Peak: Weekend Peak: Hotspot (311), Coldspot (183) - The number of significant clusters recovers from the PM dip, demonstrating that clustering is a structurally stable characteristic of the demand profile, independent of commute timing.The continued significance of Hotspots confirms that high population density remains the primary driver of concentrated origin demand.




The results are visualized to display only the statistically significant clusters (p < 0.05), with a transparent background showing the underlying trip volume distribution for context.

create_gi_map <- function(data, title){
  
  sig_data <- data %>% filter(Gi_Cluster != "Insignificant")
  
  base_map <- tm_shape(data) +
    tm_fill(
      "Total_Passenger_Trips",
      palette = "YlGnBu",
      fill_alpha = 0.1,
      fill.legend = tm_legend_hide()
    ) +
    tm_borders("black", lwd = 0.8) +
    tm_title(title) +
    tm_compass(position = c("left","top")) +
    tm_scalebar(position = c("left","bottom"))
  
  # Only adding significant layer if it exists
  if(nrow(sig_data) > 0){
    base_map <- base_map +
      tm_shape(sig_data) +
      tm_fill(
        "Gi_Cluster",
        palette = c("Hotspot" = "red", "Coldspot" = "blue"),
        fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Cluster Type")
      )
  }
  
  return(base_map)
}

# Creating maps
map_lmsa_am <- create_gi_map(lmsa_results$Weekday_AM_Peak, "LMSA: Weekday AM Peak")
map_lmsa_pm <- create_gi_map(lmsa_results$Weekday_PM_Peak, "LMSA: Weekday PM Peak")
map_lmsa_weekend <- create_gi_map(lmsa_results$Weekend_Peak, "LMSA: Weekend Peak")

Hotspots (red) are contiguous, major clusters in the residential North and Northeast, indicating dense trip origins feeding the core. Coldspots (blue) form large, unified zones in the Central and Southwest (industrial/port areas), statistically confirming them as low-origin regions. The spatial coherence of the clusters validates the existence of strong positive spatial autocorrelation at the local level.
LMSA: Weekday PM Peak Map: This visualization shows a fragmentation of the Hotspots compared to the AM Peak, which aligns with the lower count of significant Hotspots.The primary clusters remain in the North/East, but the spatial extent is reduced and less cohesive. This reflects slightly more complexity in evening trip dispersion compared to the morning convergence.The persistence of the Coldspot in the far Southwest confirms that this area consistently generates very few bus trips regardless of the time of day.
LMSA: Weekend Peak Map: The visual pattern of Hotspots remains concentrated in the major residential areas (North/East), showing that population distribution is the persistent driver of clustering. The large Coldspot zone in the Southwest is the most prominent feature, statistically identifying zones that have consistently low mobility demand across all periods. This stability suggests that planning for high-demand origins should rely on fixed geographical patterns.




The Gi* Z-scores from the three time intervals are combined into a space-time cube matrix. This prepares the data for the temporal trend test by arranging the data so that each hexagon has a time series of clustering intensity.

# Combining Gi* results across time intervals
ehsa_base <- lmsa_results$Weekday_AM_Peak %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(Hexagon_ID) %>%
  left_join(lmsa_results$Weekday_AM_Peak %>% 
              st_drop_geometry() %>% 
              select(Hexagon_ID, Gi_AM = Gi_Z_Score), by = "Hexagon_ID") %>%
  left_join(lmsa_results$Weekday_PM_Peak %>% 
              st_drop_geometry() %>% 
              select(Hexagon_ID, Gi_PM = Gi_Z_Score), by = "Hexagon_ID") %>%
  left_join(lmsa_results$Weekend_Peak %>% 
              st_drop_geometry() %>% 
              select(Hexagon_ID, Gi_Weekend = Gi_Z_Score), by = "Hexagon_ID")

# Converting to matrix for MK test
gi_matrix <- ehsa_base %>%
  select(Gi_AM, Gi_PM, Gi_Weekend) %>%
  as.matrix()

# Mann–Kendall function
compute_mk <- function(ts_vec) {
  ts_vec <- na.omit(ts_vec)
  if (length(ts_vec) == 0) return(c(Z = NA, p = NA))
  if (all(ts_vec == ts_vec[1])) return(c(Z = 0, p = 1))
  mk <- mk.test(ts_vec)
  c(Z = unname(mk$statistic[1]), p = unname(mk$p.value[1]))
}

# Applying MK test
mk_results <- apply(gi_matrix, 1, compute_mk) %>%
  t() %>%
  as_tibble(.name_repair = "minimal") %>%
  rename(MK_Z = 1, MK_p = 2)

# Merging back with base data
ehsa_df <- ehsa_base %>%
  bind_cols(mk_results)

# Significance threshold (95%)
ehsa_z95 <- qnorm(0.975)

# Output
cat("EHSA Mann-Kendall results summary:\n")

The final step categorizes each hexagon into an Emerging Hot Spot category (Intensifying, Diminishing, Persistent, etc.) by evaluating the significance of the cluster at the end of the period against the significance/direction of the Mann-Kendall trend.

ehsa_final <- ehsa_df %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    Is_Hot_End = Gi_Weekend > ehsa_z95,
    Is_Cold_End = Gi_Weekend < -ehsa_z95,
    MK_Sig = MK_p < 0.05,
    EHSA_Cluster = case_when(
      Is_Hot_End & MK_Sig & MK_Z > 0 ~ "Intensifying Hot Spot",
      Is_Hot_End & MK_Sig & MK_Z < 0 ~ "Diminishing Hot Spot",
      Is_Hot_End & !MK_Sig ~ "Persistent Hot Spot",
      Is_Cold_End & MK_Sig & MK_Z < 0 ~ "Intensifying Cold Spot",
      Is_Cold_End & MK_Sig & MK_Z > 0 ~ "Diminishing Cold Spot",
      Is_Cold_End & !MK_Sig ~ "Persistent Cold Spot",
      TRUE ~ "Insignificant"
    )
  ) %>% 
  ungroup()

# Merging with hex grid for mapping
ehsa_map_data <- hex_common_geom %>%
  left_join(ehsa_final, by = "Hexagon_ID")

# Output
cat("EHSA Cluster distribution:\n")

EHSA Cluster distribution:

                1338                  183                  311 



The zero count for Intensifying/Diminishing categories confirms the statistical conclusion that no spatial clustering pattern is undergoing rapid change across the three peak periods. The entire significant result is defined by Persistent Clusters: areas of high (Hotspot) or low (Coldspot) origin demand that have remained statistically significant clusters throughout the analyzed time series. This stability is a key planning insight: short-term bus scheduling adjustments (e.g., changes between peak times) should rely on fixed, highly persistent demand centers rather than anticipating emergent trends.

The map visually confirms the finding of temporal stability over the short analytical time window. The resulting pattern is defined entirely by Persistent Clusters (Hotspots in red/orange, Coldspots in blue/cyan) that remain statistically significant through time. The Persistent Hot Spot regions are consolidated in the Eastern and Central-Northern residential corridors, indicating areas of high,stable trip demand that require persistent priority bus servicing. The Persistent Cold Spot regions dominate the Western and Southern industrial/low-density zones, confirming stable low origin demand. The absence of any statistically validated “Intensifying” or “Diminishing” clusters is a critical insight for planners: mobility resources should prioritize addressing these geographically fixed, persistent demand centers rather than shifting resources based on short-term emerging temporal trends.

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text: The combination of LMSA and EHSA provides a powerful framework for urban mobility analysis. The LMSA identified the fixed hotspots and coldspots of trip generation during key commuting periods, serving as a baseline for current demands. The EHSA added the critical temporal dimension, revealing dynamic trends that planners can use to anticipate future demands, such as whether a current coldspot is ‘Intensifying’ towards a new travel hub, or if a busy area is ‘Diminishing’. This shift from static mapping to dynamic spatio-temporal modeling is key to designing responsive and sustainable bus networks.

geocode <- function(block, streetname) {
  base_url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search"
  address <- paste(block, streetname, sep = " ")
  query <- list("searchVal" = address, 
                "returnGeom" = "Y",
                "getAddrDetails" = "N", 
                "pageNum" = "1")
  
  res <- GET(base_url, query = query)
  restext <- content(res, as="text")
  
  output <- fromJSON(restext) %>%
    as.data.frame %>%
    select(results.LATITUDE, results.LONGITUDE)    
  return(output)
  }

title: Take Home Exercise 3
text:
Modelling HDB Resale Prices with Geographically Weighted Methods


1. Overview
This study develops a spatially informed predictive model for HDB resale prices in Singapore using transaction data from July 2024 to June 2025. Focusing on 4-room flats, the analysis integrates structural housing attributes with a rich set of geospatial accessibility measures, including proximity to hawker centres, MRT stations, parks, eldercare facilities, supermarkets, and preschool services. By converting aspatial resale records into geographically referenced point features and linking them to multiple open-source geospatial datasets, the study constructs a comprehensive analytical sandbox. Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) is applied to uncover how price determinants vary across space, revealing localised market dynamics that conventional global models cannot capture.


2. Objectives
The primary objective is to build a reproducible, spatially enhanced modelling workflow capable of predicting HDB resale prices with greater accuracy by leveraging both structural characteristics and local accessibility. Specifically, the study aims to:

Create a reliable geospatial dataset of 4-room resale flats.
Derive meaningful location-based predictors through spatial distance and within-radius computations.
Compare global OLS and local GWR models to assess spatial heterogeneity in price determinants.
Communicate findings through clear, decision-oriented geovisualisations.



3. Installing and Loading Packages

  tidyverse, sf, lwgeom, stringr, lubridate,

  readr, here, units

HDB <- read_csv(hdb_fp, show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  janitor::clean_names() %>%
  mutate(
    month = as.Date(paste0(month, "-01")),
    flat_type = toupper(flat_type),
    town = toupper(str_trim(town))
  ) %>%
  filter(flat_type == "4 ROOM") %>%
  mutate(
    remaining_lease_yrs = map_dbl(remaining_lease, ~ {
      if(is.na(.x)) return(NA_real_)
      nums <- str_extract_all(.x, "\\d+")[[1]]
      if(length(nums) == 0) return(NA_real_)
      if(length(nums) == 1) return(as.numeric(nums[1]))
      as.numeric(nums[1]) + as.numeric(nums[2]) / 12
    }),
    lease_commence_date = as.numeric(lease_commence_date),
    unit_age = year(month) - lease_commence_date,
    floor_area_sqm = as.numeric(floor_area_sqm),
    storey_mid = case_when(
      str_detect(storey_range, "TO") ~ {p <- read.table(text = gsub("TO", " ", storey_range)); rowMeans(p)},
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(str_extract(storey_range, "\\d+"))
    )
  )

message("HDB rows (4-room): ", nrow(HDB))



5. Safe SF Readers Helper Functions

safe_read_points <- function(path, target_crs = 3414) {
  if(!file.exists(path)) return(NULL)
  sf_obj <- tryCatch(st_read(path, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) return(NULL))
  if(is.null(sf_obj) || nrow(sf_obj) == 0) return(NULL)
  gtypes <- suppressWarnings(st_geometry_type(sf_obj))
  if(!all(gtypes %in% c("POINT","MULTIPOINT"))) sf_obj <- tryCatch(st_collection_extract(sf_obj, "POINT"), error = function(e) sf_obj)
  sf_obj <- tryCatch(lwgeom::st_make_valid(sf_obj), error = function(e) sf_obj)
  sf_obj <- sf_obj[!st_is_empty(sf_obj), ]
  if(is.na(st_crs(sf_obj))) st_crs(sf_obj) <- 4326
  sf_obj <- tryCatch(st_transform(sf_obj, target_crs), error = function(e) return(NULL))
  if(nrow(sf_obj) == 0) return(NULL)
  return(sf_obj)
}

safe_read_polygons <- function(path, target_crs = 3414) {
  if(!file.exists(path)) return(NULL)
  sf_obj <- tryCatch(st_read(path, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) return(NULL))
  if(is.null(sf_obj) || nrow(sf_obj) == 0) return(NULL)
  sf_obj <- tryCatch(lwgeom::st_make_valid(sf_obj), error = function(e) sf_obj)
  sf_obj <- sf_obj[!st_is_empty(sf_obj), ]
  if(is.na(st_crs(sf_obj))) st_crs(sf_obj) <- 4326
  sf_obj <- tryCatch(st_transform(sf_obj, target_crs), error = function(e) return(NULL))
  return(sf_obj)
}

9. Distance Functions

nearest_distance <- function(src, dest, colname) {
  if(is.null(dest) || nrow(dest) == 0) {src[[colname]] <- 999; return(src)}
  if(st_crs(src) != st_crs(dest)) dest <- st_transform(dest, st_crs(src))
  idx <- st_nearest_feature(src, dest)
  d <- st_distance(src, dest[idx, ], by_element = TRUE)
  src[[colname]] <- as.numeric(d)/1000
  return(src)
}

within_count <- function(src, dest, dist_m) {
  if(is.null(dest) || nrow(dest) == 0) return(rep(0, nrow(src)))
  if(st_crs(src) != st_crs(dest)) dest <- st_transform(dest, st_crs(src))
  lengths(st_is_within_distance(src, dest, dist = dist_m))
}

13. OLS Baseline

drop_singular_predictors <- function(df, response) {
  keep_vars <- setdiff(names(df), response)
  formula_try <- as.formula(paste(response, "~", paste(keep_vars, collapse = "+")))
  repeat {
    model <- try(lm(formula_try, data = df), silent = TRUE)
    if(inherits(model, "try-error")) break
    coefs_na <- names(coef(model))[is.na(coef(model))]
    if(length(coefs_na) == 0) break
    keep_vars <- setdiff(keep_vars, coefs_na[1])
    if(length(keep_vars) == 0) break
    formula_try <- as.formula(paste(response, "~", paste(keep_vars, collapse = "+")))
  }
  list(df = df[, c(response, keep_vars), drop = FALSE], predictors = keep_vars)
}

  HDB_sp <- as(HDB_geo_safe,"Spatial")
  gwr_bw <- bw.gwr(as.formula(paste("resale_price ~", paste(gwr_vars_safe, collapse=" + "))),
                   data = HDB_sp, approach="AICc", kernel="bisquare", adaptive=TRUE)
  gwr_fit <- gwr.basic(as.formula(paste("resale_price ~", paste(gwr_vars_safe, collapse=" + "))),
                       data = HDB_sp, bw=gwr_bw, kernel="bisquare", adaptive=TRUE)
  gwr_sf <- st_as_sf(gwr_fit$SDF)
  saveRDS(gwr_sf, "data/rds/gwr_results.rds")
} else gwr_sf <- NULL

library(tmap)

# Setting static plotting mode
tmap_mode("plot")

# Fixed plotting function for numeric SF variables
plot_numeric_sf_fixed <- function(sf_obj, var, title = NULL, size = 0.5, palette = "RdYlBu") {
  if(is.null(sf_obj) || nrow(sf_obj) == 0) return(NULL)
  if(!(var %in% names(sf_obj))) return(NULL)
  
  # Ensuring numeric
  sf_obj[[var]] <- as.numeric(sf_obj[[var]])
  
  tm_shape(sf_obj) +
    tm_dots(
      col = var,               # color by variable
      size = size,             # fixed size in map units
      palette = palette,
      auto.palette.mapping = FALSE, # disable auto-scaling
      title = var
    ) +
    tm_layout(
      legend.outside = TRUE,
      frame = FALSE
    ) +
    tm_title(title)
}

# GWR outputs
if(exists("gwr_sf") && !is.null(gwr_sf)) {
  
  # Identifying numeric coefficients (exclude residuals, Local_R2, X, Y)
  coef_cols <- setdiff(
    names(gwr_sf)[sapply(st_drop_geometry(gwr_sf), is.numeric)],
    c("residual", "Local_R2", "X", "Y")
  )
  
  # Plotting first coefficient as example
  if(length(coef_cols) > 0) {
    map_gwr_coef <- plot_numeric_sf_fixed(
      gwr_sf, coef_cols[1], paste("GWR coefficient:", coef_cols[1])
    )
    if(!is.null(map_gwr_coef)) print(map_gwr_coef)
  }
  
  # Plotting GWR residuals
  if("residual" %in% names(gwr_sf)) {
    map_gwr_resid <- plot_numeric_sf_fixed(gwr_sf, "residual", "GWR residuals")
    if(!is.null(map_gwr_resid)) print(map_gwr_resid)
  }
  
  # Plotting GWR Local R2
  if("Local_R2" %in% names(gwr_sf)) {
    map_gwr_r2 <- plot_numeric_sf_fixed(gwr_sf, "Local_R2", "GWR Local R2")
    if(!is.null(map_gwr_r2)) print(map_gwr_r2)
  }
}
